content_html:
Pet urine odor persists when liquid reaches seams, porous materials, or layers below the surface that routine mopping cannot reach. The right method depends on whether the floor is sealed, wood, laminate, stone, or a porous material such as concrete.

Blot fresh urine instead of spreading it

Press with paper towels or absorbent cloths and switch to clean areas until little moisture transfers. Avoid scrubbing in circles over seams because that can push liquid farther into edges and gaps.

Use a cleaner compatible with the floor finish

Enzymatic cleaners can help break down organic residues, but they must be safe for the specific flooring. Test first in an inconspicuous spot and never mix cleaning products, especially bleach with acidic or ammonia-containing cleaners.

Check seams, baseboards, and edges for hidden contamination

If odor remains strongest at a seam or edge, urine may have penetrated below the finish. On swollen laminate or wood, repeated surface cleaning will not correct contaminated underlayment or subfloor material.

Replace damaged material when contamination is underneath

Odor that returns during humid weather or after repeated cleaning may be coming from below the finished floor. Removing and replacing affected boards, underlayment, or sealing damaged substrate may be the only durable solution after deep contamination.
